text: There's no single server called "the blockchain" to call. Ethereum is thousands of independently run nodes, each holding a full copy of chain state, each answering JSON-RPC requests. Talking to the chain always means talking to one specific node.

Chainlist.org is a live directory of public RPC endpoints per chain — because there's no single answer to "what node do I call." Each entry shows its own current block height and latency, so you can compare them.
Running your own node is real infrastructure — hundreds of gigabytes, hours to sync, a server you'd keep patched forever. Most teams pay a node provider instead, like Infura, now part of MetaMask.
Sign up and a provider hands you an RPC endpoint URL with your API key baked right in, plus a dashboard for watching live request volume and success rate for your app.
Point a library at that URL and that's the whole setup — you're talking to a real synced node without running one yourself.
A managed provider is almost always the right default — no infrastructure, generous free tiers, dozens of chains behind one account. Next up: reading real chain data with ethers.js and viem.
